summary: This document defines a new test command, duplicate, for the Sieve email filtering language. It lets filters detect duplicate deliveries, such as those caused by mailing list subscriptions or redirected addresses, normally by checking message IDs against earlier delivered mail.

eli5.summary: If you get two copies of the same letter, you would like to throw the second one away. This RFC gives email filters a way to notice they have seen a message before.

questions: what is the sieve duplicate test
how to detect duplicate emails with sieve
what does the sieve handle argument do
subtitle: A Sieve test that lets an email filter notice it has already seen a message and handle the copy.

tldr.problem: Mailing lists, crossposting and redirected addresses often deliver the same message to a user more than once, and Sieve scripts had no way to tell that a message was seen before.
tldr.mechanism: The "duplicate" test computes a unique ID for the message (normally its Message-ID), checks it against an internal tracking list built by earlier script runs, and adds it to the list when the script finishes successfully.
tldr.outcome: Scripts can discard, flag or file duplicates, or reuse the same idea for other string-keyed tasks such as rate-limiting notifications. The unique ID can come from any header or any string the script builds.

today: RFC 7352 is a Proposed Standard (September 2014) and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on the Sieve language in RFC 5228.

sections.title: Why Duplicates Happen
sections.content:
RFC 7352 extends the Sieve email filtering language defined in RFC 5228 with one new test, duplicate. It tracks whether a text string was seen before by the delivery agent in an earlier execution of the Sieve script.

The RFC lists common sources of duplicates. A list member replies to both the user and the list, so the user gets one copy directly and one through the list. Someone crossposts to several lists the user has joined. Or several redirected addresses all point to one main account and a contact writes to more than one of them. With the new test, a user can discard such copies, mark them as seen, or file them in a special folder.

Duplicates are normally spotted with the Message-ID header field, which is required to be unique for each message. The test is flexible enough to use other criteria, such as the subject line or parts of the body, as long as the tracked value is a string.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the same letter reaches your mailbox twice because it was sent to you through two routes. This tool helps a filter spot the second copy.

sections.title: How the duplicate Test Works
sections.content:
The syntax is duplicate with optional :handle, :header or :uniqueid, :seconds and :last arguments. The test identifies the message by a unique ID and keeps track of which IDs were seen by a duplicate test during an earlier Sieve execution. It evaluates to true if the ID was seen before and false if not.

As a side effect, the unique ID is added to an internal duplicate-tracking list once the Sieve execution finishes successfully. Implementations MUST only update the list on success. Otherwise a failed run would record the ID, and the next delivery attempt of the same message would wrongly look like a duplicate, which could silently discard it.

The test MUST only compare against IDs from previous executions, never IDs seen earlier in the current run. So all duplicate tests with identical arguments in one run, including those in included scripts, give the same answer. The RFC also warns about a race: if a duplicate is delivered in parallel before the list is updated, it could be missed. Locking can help, but cases where the test wrongly yields true MUST be prevented.

The list is updated only when the test is actually evaluated. If it sits inside a control structure or is not the first item of an allof or anyof list, results may be unexpected.
sections.eli5: The filter writes down each letter's number only after it has finished handling the letter. That way a letter that got lost halfway is not mistaken for a copy later.

sections.title: Choosing the Unique ID
sections.content:
By default the unique ID is the content of the Message-ID header field. With :header, it is the value of the named header field (the field name is not part of the ID). With :uniqueid, it is the string given as the argument. :header and :uniqueid are mutually exclusive, and using both MUST trigger an error.

When the ID comes straight from a header, the implementation MUST first unfold the header line, convert the value to UTF-8 if possible (otherwise leave it unchanged), and trim leading and trailing whitespace. If the header occurs several times, only the first occurrence is used. If it is missing, or the header name is invalid, the test MUST yield false and leave the tracking list unmodified; an invalid name is not an error.

With :uniqueid the script can build the string with the variables extension, and with foreverypart and extracttext to pull text from the body. Matching against the list is case-sensitive; to get case-insensitive behavior, the script can normalize the value to upper or lower case with set.

The RFC notes that Message-ID is assumed to be globally unique, as RFC 5322 requires, but in practice that may not hold, so false duplicates can occur. An alternative ID via :header or :uniqueid addresses that.
sections.eli5: You can tell the filter which part of the letter to use as its number: the usual stamp, a different label, or something you make up yourself from the letter.

sections.title: Handles and Expiry
sections.content:
All tracked values are shared by default, whatever their source. These three scripts are equivalent and match the same entry: plain duplicate, duplicate :header "message-id", and duplicate :uniqueid "${0}" with the value taken from the Message-ID. The :handle argument overrides that. A message counts as a duplicate only if the ID was seen earlier by a test with the same handle, so unrelated tests do not interfere. One suggested implementation is to store a hash of the unique ID and the handle.

Entries should not live forever. Implementations SHOULD let entries expire, and :seconds sets the timeout. If it is omitted, an appropriate default MUST be used, and the RFC says around 7 days is usually appropriate. Sites SHOULD impose a maximum; a larger :seconds value is silently replaced by that maximum, not treated as an error. A :seconds value of zero makes the test yield false unconditionally.

Without :last, expiry is measured from when the entry was first created, so later duplicates do not extend it. With :last, it is measured from the last execution that checked the entry, so the entry survives as long as duplicates keep arriving within the timeout. Mixing different :seconds or :last values for the same ID and handle in one run gives undefined behavior.
sections.eli5: You can keep separate notebooks for separate jobs, and each note in a notebook gets erased after a while. You choose whether the timer starts when the note is first written or restarts every time a copy shows up.

sections.title: Examples from the RFC
sections.content:
Example 1 files duplicates into Trash/Duplicate (created automatically with the mailbox extension) so the user can recover them. Example 2 handles alerts from several monitoring systems: the Message-IDs differ, so the script matches subjects like ALERT: *, uses the event description as :uniqueid with :seconds 60, and marks duplicates as seen.

Example 3 limits XMPP notifications to at most one per sender every 30 minutes (:seconds 1800) using the envelope sender as the unique ID. It can be extended to combine sender and subject so different subjects still notify. Example 4 uses :handle values notifier and support so that tests keyed on X-Event-ID and X-Ticket-ID cannot match each other's values.
sections.eli5: The examples show a filter tossing copies into a special folder, quieting repeated alarms, and sending at most one text message per person every half hour.

sections.title: Other Extensions and Capability
sections.content:
The test does not directly support the index or mime extensions, so no :index or :mime arguments are added. The :uniqueid argument with variables achieves the same result indirectly.

Scripts normally run at final delivery. With the imapsieve extension they run when an IMAP server performs operations on the message store, and the semantics of duplicate there are left undefined, so implementations SHOULD NOT allow it in that context. An implementation advertises the capability string duplicate, which IANA registered with the contact address Sieve mailing list.
sections.eli5: The tool works when mail first arrives. It is not meant for the moments when you shuffle mail around afterward.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A flood of unique messages could make the tracking list grow without bound, so implementations SHOULD limit the number of entries and discard the oldest first. Message IDs are not necessarily unique, whether from benign generators or from an attacker injecting a message with the properties the filter uses, so scripts should be conservative about actions taken when duplicates are identified only by message ID.

The list can hold privacy-sensitive information such as message IDs, subject lines and body text. Implementations SHOULD protect it by hashing and/or by access control equal to that of the messages. Even so, someone with access to the list can ask whether messages with certain IDs were received, and a user who deleted a message may not expect a record to remain. The RFC suggests a shorter default expiry may be appropriate where users are trying to limit traceability.
sections.eli5: The notebook could fill up or reveal what mail you got, so it should be kept private, limited in size and cleaned out regularly.
